source.title: Towards joint scaling laws with optimal batch size schedules
source.authors: Jiaxiang Li; Zhi-Qi Bu; Shi-Yun Xu

record.file_problem: Supplied full paper text, including appendices; no garbling or cutoff apparent.
record.tranche_reason: Compares dynamic and static batch-size schedules using validation loss and downstream held-out evaluations, a different intervention and measure from the claim’s large-batch comparisons.
record.gate_note: Results bear on V5 through dynamic-versus-static batch-size comparisons. The paper does not report training error alongside held-out error, so it does not measure the train–test gap. Cited prior work on large-batch generalization is not extracted as this paper’s result.
record.test_reason: Figure 1 bears narrowly on V5's recipe-adaptation qualification: under fixed compute, dynamically scheduled larger batches reach the static baseline's loss with fewer iterations. Most extracted rows instead compare dynamic and static schedules without identifying a larger-versus-smaller average batch contrast, so they do not independently test V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase captures the authors' main conclusion: their convex-theory-derived batch schedule improves loss and scaling efficiency relative to static scheduling. Qualify empirical consistency: downstream VLM scores are mixed. The scheduling advantage vanishes in their pure-bf16 experiment and tends to zero theoretically as base batch size approaches infinity, but remains present at the tested 8× base batch.
record.recipe_differences: The study derives and tests an optimal dynamic batch-size schedule, comparing it with static batch-size baselines; it does not reproduce the original large-batch interventions or train–test-gap measures.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by model, downstream benchmark, learning-rate schedule, training precision, base batch size, and training regime. The reported advantage vanishes in half-precision; performance is mixed across VLM benchmark tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Dynamic scheduling improves most downstream scores and reported perplexities relative to static scheduling, with several lower VLM scores.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Redistributing a fixed token budget across training steps can improve held-out performance relative to a constant batch size at the same average batch size.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched learning-rate-to-batch-size trajectories and token budgets, learning-rate scheduling achieves lower validation loss in all nine comparisons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The learning-rate-to-batch-size ratio alone does not determine language-model training outcomes.

record.problems: The study reports held-out loss and downstream metrics but not training error, so it cannot quantify the generalization gap. Some comparisons are described in figures without exact values, and uncertainty estimates are not stated. VLM benchmark results are mixed.
record.rows_left_out: No reported comparisons of dynamic versus static batch size were left out. Cited results from prior work were excluded.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label generalization, and chance performance on held-out random labels.
Width beyond zero training error and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under comparable tuning budgets; using AdamW and Muon is not this comparison.

The extracted rows do not establish the fixed-batch large-versus-small penalty or its threshold. Longer training, learning-rate scaling with warmup, and normalization or regularization remedies are not isolated. Figure 1 tests only the possibility of preserving held-out loss with larger average batches through scheduling.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on training-set size, augmentation, or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm or margin measures.
Removing memorized training examples versus random removal.

missing.what: Separate rows for the larger-average dynamic-batch comparisons against smaller static batches: matched loss with 62.5% fewer iterations for Llama3 and 37.5% fewer for Qwen3 at fixed compute. Record batch sizes, horizons, and the equal token budget explicitly.

Fixed-compute base-batch ablation across 1×, 2×, 4×, and 8× batches, with 1× equal to 128k tokens. Extract held-out endpoints across batch sizes to assess V5 directly. The supplied text preserves within-size dynamic/static improvements but does not make the cross-size endpoint values readable.

record.verdict_notes: Training error is unnecessary for V5, which concerns held-out performance under controlled training budgets. Its absence prevents measuring a train–test gap but is not grounds for rejecting the relevant fixed-compute comparison. Figure-only reporting is likewise not itself a scope limitation.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Convolutional versus fully connected image models.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD held-out performance.

Does not compare small versus large batches across a workload-dependent threshold under fixed epoch budgets, or isolate the effects of learning-rate scaling, warmup, normalization, or explicit regularization. It tests dynamic versus static schedules and reports held-out metrics.
Sharpness and other measured properties as predictors of the train–test gap.
